claim: The pre-Bötzinger complex (pre-BötC) is a medullary region generating the inspiratory phase of breathing in mammals.
source: The pre-BötC is a medullary region representing an excitatory kernel circuit of the respiratory CPG in mammals that is critically involved in generating the inspiratory phase of respiration (Smith et al., 1991; Smith et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2009; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing the role of pre-BötC in respiration.

claim: A progressive increase of neuronal excitability in medullary slices containing the pre-BötC produces mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs) characterized by large amplitude population bursts alternating with a series of small amplitude bursts.
source: A progressive increase of neuronal excitability in medullary slices containing the pre-BötC produces mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs) characterized by large amplitude population bursts alternating with a series of small amplitude bursts.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MMOs emerge within a heterogeneous excitatory neural network because of progressive neuronal recruitment and synchronization.
source: Using two different computational models, we demonstrate that MMOs emerge within a heterogeneous excitatory neural network because of progressive neuronal recruitment and synchronization.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The MMO pattern depends on the distributed neuronal excitability, the density and weights of network interconnections, and the cellular properties underlying endogenous bursting.
source: The MMO pattern depends on the distributed neuronal excitability, the density and weights of network interconnections, and the cellular properties underlying endogenous bursting.
evidence: This is demonstrated through systematic parameter variations in the computational models.

claim: The cellular properties underlying endogenous bursting should provide a reduction of spiking frequency within neuronal bursts with increasing burst frequency.
source: Critically, the latter should provide a reduction of spiking frequency within neuronal bursts with increasing burst frequency and a dependence of the after-burst recovery period on burst amplitude.
evidence: This is a critical property identified through modeling and analysis.

claim: The cellular properties underlying endogenous bursting should provide a dependence of the after-burst recovery period on burst amplitude.
source: Critically, the latter should provide a reduction of spiking frequency within neuronal bursts with increasing burst frequency and a dependence of the after-burst recovery period on burst amplitude.
evidence: This is a critical property identified through modeling and analysis.

claim: Heterogeneity naturally leads to complex dynamics in rhythmic neuronal populations.
source: Our study highlights a novel mechanism by which heterogeneity naturally leads to complex dynamics in rhythmic neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a key conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs) represent rhythmic behaviors of dynamical systems characterized by an alternation between large amplitude (LA) and small amplitude (SA) oscillations.
source: Mixed-mode oscillations (MMOs) represent rhythmic behaviors of dynamical systems characterized by an alternation between large amplitude (LA) and small amplitude (SA) oscillations (Desroches et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to prior work.

claim: MMOs have been observed in populations of neurons in the entorhinal cortex.
source: The latter include populations of neurons in the entorhinal cortex (Dickson et al., 2000; Yoshida and Alonso, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: MMOs have been observed in hippocampal neurons.
source: hippocampal neurons (Winson, 1978)
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: MMOs have been observed in dopaminergic neurons.
source: dopaminergic neurons (Medvedev et al., 2003; Medvedev and Cisternas, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental observations.

claim: MMOs have been observed in neurons of the medullary pre-Bötzinger complex.
source: neurons of the medullary pre-Bötzinger complex (Del Negro et al., 2002c)
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: MMOs have been observed in vibrissa motoneurons in rats.
source: vibrissa motoneurons (Golomb, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: MMOs have been observed in spinal motoneurons in rats.
source: spinal motoneurons (Iglesias et al., 2011) in rats.
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: Heterogeneity in the quantitative features of neurons is likely a ubiquitous property of central pattern generator circuits.
source: Heterogeneity in the quantitative features of the neurons involved is likely a ubiquitous property of such circuits (Butera et al., 1999b; Marder, 2011; Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on neural heterogeneity.

claim: The pre-BötC can generate rhythmic bursting activity in vitro, in medullary slices containing this structure.
source: The pre-BötC can generate rhythmic bursting activity in vitro, in medullary slices containing this structure (Koshiya and Smith, 1999; Del Negro et al., 2001; Rigatto et al., 2001; Thoby-Brisson and Ramirez, 2001)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental observations.

claim: The pre-BötC can generate rhythmic bursting activity in isolated 'islands' extracted from medullary slices.
source: and even in isolated 'islands' extracted from these slices (Johnson et al., 2001; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to Figure 1A showing experimental data.

claim: Rhythmic activity in the pre-BötC is typically induced by elevating the extracellular concentration of potassium ([K+]out) up to 7–9 mM.
source: This rhythmic activity is typically induced by elevating the extracellular concentration of potassium ([K+]out) up to 7–9 mM, which putatively increases neuronal excitability (Koshiya and Smith, 1999; Lieske et al., 2000; Del Negro et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 2001; Thoby-Brisson and Ramirez, 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental protocols.

claim: Elevating extracellular potassium concentration to 7-9 mM putatively increases neuronal excitability in the pre-BötC.
source: This rhythmic activity is typically induced by elevating the extracellular concentration of potassium ([K+]out) up to 7–9 mM, which putatively increases neuronal excitability (Koshiya and Smith, 1999; Lieske et al., 2000; Del Negro et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 2001; Thoby-Brisson and Ramirez, 2001).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Bursts in the XII root represent the synchronized activity of pre-BötC neurons.
source: Simultaneous optical recordings from individual neurons and XII output have shown that bursts in the XII root represent the synchronized activity of pre-BötC neurons (Koshiya and Smith, 1999; Figure 1C1,C2)
evidence: Supported by citation and reference to experimental data in Figure 1C1,C2.

claim: The amplitude of XII bursts depends on the number of pre-BötC neurons involved.
source: and the amplitude of XII bursts clearly depends on the number of pre-BötC neurons involved.
evidence: This is an inference from experimental observations.

claim: A progressive increase in [K+]out in slices containing the pre-BötC evokes complex population MMOs characterized by amplitude modulation, with large amplitude (LA) bursts alternating with a series of small amplitude (SA) bursts.
source: Interestingly, a progressive increase in [K+]out in slices containing the pre-BötC evokes complex population MMOs characterized by amplitude modulation, with large amplitude (LA) bursts alternating with a series of small amplitude (SA) bursts (Koshiya and Smith, 1999; Del Negro et al., 2002c; Kam et al., 2013) (see Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: An amplitude irregularity similar to the MMOs recorded from the pre-BötC in vitro has been observed during acute intermittent hypoxia simulated in vitro.
source: An amplitude irregularity similar to the MMOs recorded from the pre-BötC in vitro has also been observed during acute intermittent hypoxia simulated in vitro (Zanella et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental observation.

claim: Similar pathological patterns of breathing have been observed in vivo in association with myocardial infarcts, obstructive sleep apneas, apneas of prematurity, Rett syndrome, and sudden infant death syndrome.
source: Similar pathological patterns of breathing have been observed in vivo in association with different diseases, such as myocardial infarcts, obstructive sleep apneas, apneas of prematurity, Rett syndrome, and sudden infant death syndrome (Zanella et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical observations.

claim: Intracellular recordings from individual pre-BötC neurons in rhythmically active slices show a range of resting membrane potentials and other quantitative properties among individual neurons.
source: Intracellular recordings from individual pre-BötC neurons in rhythmically active slices show a range of resting membrane potentials and other quantitative properties among individual neurons (Del Negro et al., 2001; Del Negro et al., 2002a; Peña et al., 2004; Koizumi and Smith, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental observations.

claim: Neurons with more negative resting membrane potentials usually generate bursting activity that is fully consistent with, and reflected in, XII output activity.
source: Neurons with more negative resting membrane potentials usually generate bursting activity that is fully consistent with, and reflected in, XII output activity, whereas neurons with less negative resting membrane potentials demonstrate higher burst frequencies and often generate 'ectopic' busts not reflected in the XII output (see example in Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by reference to experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: Neurons with less negative resting membrane potentials demonstrate higher burst frequencies and often generate 'ectopic' bursts not reflected in the XII output.
source: Neurons with more negative resting membrane potentials usually generate bursting activity that is fully consistent with, and reflected in, XII output activity, whereas neurons with less negative resting membrane potentials demonstrate higher burst frequencies and often generate 'ectopic' busts not reflected in the XII output (see example in Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by reference to experimental data in Figure 1B.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of synaptic transmission within the pre-BötC by CNQX results in a reduction and desynchronization of neuronal activity within the pre-BötC, with no activity in the hypoglossal output.
source: Pharmacological blockade of synaptic transmission within the pre-BötC by 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) results in a reduction and desynchronization of neuronal activity within the pre-BötC, with no activity in the hypoglossal output (see example in Figure 1C1,C2).
evidence: Supported by reference to experimental data in Figure 1C1,C2.

claim: The computational model of the pre-BötC consists of 100 neurons described in the Hodgkin-Huxley style, with sparse excitatory synaptic interconnections between neurons.
source: we modeled the pre-BötC as an excitatory network consisting of 100 neurons described in the Hodgkin-Huxley style, with sparse excitatory synaptic interconnections between neurons.
evidence: This describes the computational model structure used in the study.

claim: The intrinsic bursting properties of neurons in the model were based on the persistent (slowly inactivating) sodium current, INaP.
source: The intrinsic bursting properties of these neurons were based on the persistent (slowly inactivating) sodium current, INaP (Butera et al., 1999a; Butera et al., 1999b; Del Negro et al., 2001; Rybak et al., 2003a; Rybak et al., 2003b; Rybak et al., 2004; Rybak et al., 2014; Dunmyre and Rubin, 2010; Jasinski et al., 2013; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the computational model, supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: In the absence of coupling, the population contained silent neurons, as well as neurons with bursting and tonic activities.
source: In the absence of coupling (when all weights of connections were set to zero), the population contained silent neurons, as well as neurons with bursting and tonic activities (Figure 2A1).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 2A1.

claim: Neurons with the most negative EL values were silent.
source: This figure shows that neurons with the most negative EL values were silent (neurons with ID numbers from 1 to 49)
evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claim: Neurons with intermediate EL exhibited bursting activity with burst frequency increasing with EL.
source: neurons with intermediate EL exhibited bursting activity with burst frequency increasing with EL (neurons 50–94)
evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claim: Neurons with greatest EL displayed tonic spiking.
source: and neurons with greatest EL displayed tonic spiking (neurons 95–100).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claim: The lack of network interactions resulted in asynchronous neuronal activity and the corresponding integrated population histogram lacked phasic modulation.
source: The lack of network interactions resulted in asynchronous neuronal activity and the corresponding integrated population histogram lacked phasic modulation (Figure 2A3).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 2A3.

claim: When relatively weak and sparse excitatory synaptic connections among neurons were incorporated in the model, the patterns of population activity and integrated output dramatically changed.
source: The patterns of population activity and integrated output dramatically changed when relatively weak and sparse excitatory synaptic connections among neurons were incorporated in the model (Figure 2B1–B3).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 2B1-B3.

claim: In the coupled case, overlapping clusters (sub-populations) of neurons with synchronized bursting generate MMOs characterized by alternating LA and SA population bursts.
source: The raster plot of the same sorted neurons in this coupled case (Figure 2B2) shows the presence of overlapping clusters (sub-populations) of neurons with synchronized bursting, which generate MMOs characterized by alternating LA and SA population bursts (Figure 2B3).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 2B2-B3.

claim: While the burst frequency increased with the neuronal excitability, the spike frequency within the burst changed in an inverse manner, i.e., decreased with increasing neuronal excitability.
source: An important feature of all neurons operating in bursting mode is illustrated in Figure 3A3 (uncoupled case): while the burst frequency (blue curve) increased with the neuronal excitability (bottom-up), the spike frequency within the burst (red curve) changed in an inverse manner, i.e., decreased with increasing neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is a key finding from the computational model shown in Figure 3A3.

claim: The reduction of spike frequency within the bursts in more excited neurons limited their ability to synchronize and recruit other neurons' activity in the coupled case.
source: This reduction of spike frequency within the bursts in more excited neurons limited their ability to synchronize and recruit other neurons' activity in the coupled case (see below).
evidence: This is an inference from the computational model results.

claim: Several clusters of neurons with synchronous bursting activity emerged dynamically in the coupled population.
source: Several clusters of neurons with synchronous bursting activity emerged dynamically in the population.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claim: Clusters differed by the number of the population bursts in which they participated, which in turn defined the amplitude of integrated population bursts.
source: Clusters differed by the number of the population bursts in which they participated (panel B1), which in turn defined the amplitude of integrated population bursts (panel C1).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claim: Generation of low-frequency LA bursts involved synchronization of many neurons and included those with low excitability (most negative EL).
source: Generation of low-frequency LA bursts involved synchronization of many neurons and included those with low excitability (most negative EL) (Figure 3B1,B2,C1).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 3B1,B2,C1.

claim: The sub-population of low excitability neurons do not contribute to SA bursts.
source: Note that the sub-population of low excitability neurons, colored red, do not contribute to SA bursts.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model analysis.

claim: The sub-population of neurons with low excitability cannot be recruited by other sub-populations until sufficient recovery of bursting capability in the low excitability neurons has occurred.
source: We further find that the sub-population of neurons with low excitability (colored red) cannot be recruited by other sub-populations (participating in SA bursts), and hence cannot generate LA bursts, until sufficient recovery of bursting capability in the low excitability neurons (defined by the INaP inactivation variable hNaP) has occurred.
evidence: This is a key finding from the computational model analysis.

claim: The generation of LA bursts and the durations of their interburst intervals (IBIs) are mostly defined by the operation of an intrinsic burst-supporting mechanism in the less excitable neurons, rather than by variations in the intensity of their recruitment by the activity of highly excitable neurons involved in SA bursts.
source: This observation suggests that with fixed parameter values, even though the low excitability neurons do not burst when uncoupled, the generation of LA bursts and the durations of their interburst intervals (IBIs) are mostly defined by the operation of an intrinsic burst-supporting mechanism in the less excitable neurons, rather than by variations in the intensity of their recruitment by the activity of highly excitable neurons involved in SA bursts.
evidence: This is an inference from the computational model results.

claim: When either weights or probability of connections were increased, the frequency of LA bursts increased and the number of SA bursts between successive LA bursts decreased.
source: When either weights (Figure 4A1,A2,B1) or probability of connections (Figure 4A1,A3,B2) were increased, the frequency of LA bursts increased and the number of SA bursts between successive LA bursts decreased.
evidence: This is a result from systematic parameter variations in the computational model shown in Figure 4.

claim: At the lowest weights (w = 1.0), only irregular SA bursts were observed because of insufficient neuronal synchronization.
source: At the lowest weights (w = 1.0), only irregular SA bursts were observed because of insufficient neuronal synchronization (top trace, Figure 4B1).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model shown in Figure 4B1.

claim: No parameter sets produced stable regimes with more than five SA bursts per one LA burst.
source: no parameter sets produced stable regimes with more than five SA bursts per one LA burst.
evidence: This is a result from systematic parameter exploration in the computational model.

claim: Simulations showed increased IBIs following the LA bursts, relative to IBIs observed after SA bursts, in all instances of MMOs.
source: Furthermore, our simulations showed increased IBIs following the LA bursts, relative to IBIs observed after SA bursts, in all instances of MMOs (Figures 2B3,3C1, and 4B1,B2).
evidence: This is a consistent result across multiple simulations shown in the referenced figures.

claim: A reduced model was developed consisting of three neurons with mutual excitatory synaptic interactions.
source: The model consisted of three neurons with mutual excitatory synaptic interactions (see Figure 5A1).
evidence: This describes the structure of the reduced model.

claim: Each model neuron in the reduced model represented a sub-population of spiking neurons with a particular level of excitability.
source: It was considered that each model neuron represented a sub-population of spiking neurons with a particular level of excitability.
evidence: This describes the conceptual basis of the reduced model.

claim: In the reduced model without coupling, neuron 1 (high excitability, HE) engaged in high frequency bursting, neuron 2 (moderate excitability, ME) engaged in low frequency bursting, and neuron 3 (low excitability, LE) was silent.
source: EL values were distributed such that in the absence of coupling, neuron 1 (high excitability, HE) engaged in high frequency bursting, neuron 2 (moderate excitability, ME) engaged in low frequency bursting with no special frequency relation to the bursting of the HE neuron, and neuron 3 (low excitability, LE) was silent; the three neurons' summed activity provided a representation of network output (Figure 5B1,C1,D1,E1).
evidence: This describes the behavior of the reduced model without coupling, shown in Figure 5B1.

claim: When connection weights were progressively increased in the reduced model, the network underwent a series of regime transitions progressing from only SA bursts to only LA bursts.
source: Similarly to the previous model, when connection weights were progressively increased, the network underwent a series of regime transitions progressing from only SA bursts (Figure 5B1,B2) to only LA bursts (Figure 5E1,E2).
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model shown in Figure 5.

claim: LA bursts involved activation of all neurons and occurred exactly on the cycles when the LE neuron activated.
source: As in the previous model, LA bursts involved activation of all neurons and occurred exactly on the cycles when the LE neuron activated (Figure 5C1,C2,D1,D2,E1,E2).
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model shown in Figure 5.

claim: For each neuron, when it was silent, there was a level of synaptic input that caused its activation.
source: A key point was that for each neuron, when it was silent, there was a level of synaptic input that caused its activation.
evidence: This is a key mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claim: The level of synaptic input required for activation depended on the degree of INaP deinactivation in the neuron, quantified by hNaP, as well as on its excitability.
source: This level depended on the degree of INaP deinactivation in the neuron, quantified by hNaP, as well as on its excitability.
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claim: The LE neuron is activated if the trajectory rises above the left knee, or local maximum, of the V3-nullcline.
source: The LE neuron is activated if the trajectory rises above the left knee, or local maximum, of the V3-nullcline (analogously to the sample trajectory in Figure 5B3).
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 5B3.

claim: Incoming synaptic excitation lowers the V3-nullcline.
source: Incoming synaptic excitation lowers the V3-nullcline (Figure 5C3,D3,E3), a well-known effect known as fast threshold modulation (Somers and Kopell, 1993)
evidence: This is a known mechanism supported by citation and demonstrated in the reduced model.

claim: If a synaptic input lowers the left knee below the current value of hNaP3, then the LE neuron is activated.
source: If a synaptic input lowers the left knee below the current value of hNaP3, then the LE neuron is activated (e.g., Figure 5C3, marked with 'iv').
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 5C3.

claim: The activation of the LE neuron depends on the recovery of hNaP3 when input arrives, and hence on the rate of recovery of hNaP3 relative to the frequency of input arrival.
source: Therefore, the activation of the LE neuron depends on the recovery of hNaP3 when input arrives, and hence on the rate of recovery of hNaP3 relative to the frequency of input arrival.
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claim: When synaptic weights were increased, the correspondingly larger excitatory input moved the V3-nullcline to lower hNaP3 values, allowing activation of the LE neuron with less recovery time and hence with fewer input cycles.
source: When synaptic weights were increased, the correspondingly larger excitatory input moved the V3-nullcline to lower hNaP3 values, allowing activation of the LE neuron with less recovery time (increase of hNaP3) and hence with fewer input cycles.
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claim: A discrete number of activations of the HE and ME neurons is needed before hNaP3 recovers to a level from which the LE neuron can activate, which gives rise to the quantal nature of the MMO patterns.
source: In all cases, a discrete number of activations of the HE and ME neurons is needed before hNaP3 recovers to a level from which the LE neuron can activate (Figure 5C3,D3,E3), which gives rise to the quantal nature of the MMO patterns (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a key mechanistic insight explaining the quantal nature of MMOs.

claim: Critical connection weights that separate regimes correspond to tangencies to curves of knees for neurons.
source: Critical connection weights that separate regimes correspond to tangencies to such curves.
evidence: This is a mathematical insight from the reduced model analysis.

claim: The transition from 1:1 to 1:2 regimes as w is decreased occurs when the ME neuron no longer can activate on every cycle.
source: For example, the transition from 1:1 to 1:2 regimes as w is decreased occurs when the ME neuron no longer can activate on every cycle (Figure 5D1).
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 5D1.

claim: At the transitional weights from 1:1 to 1:2 regimes, the trajectory, projected to the (input2, hNaP2) plane, exhibits a tangency to the curve of knees for the ME neuron.
source: At the transitional weights, the trajectory, projected to the (input2, hNaP2) plane, exhibits a tangency to the curve of knees for the ME neuron (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The transition from 1:2 to 1:4 occurs when the LE neuron no longer can activate on every second cycle.
source: Similarly, the next transition, from 1:2 to 1:4, occurs when the LE neuron no longer can activate on every second cycle.
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis.

claim: At the weights for the transition from 1:2 to 1:4, the projection of the trajectory to the (input3, hNaP3) plane exhibits a tangency to the curve of knees for the LE neuron.
source: Thus, at the weights for this transition, the projection of the trajectory to the (input3, hNaP3) plane exhibits a tangency to the curve of knees for the LE neuron (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A change in the excitability of the LE neuron alone could alter the V3-nullclines and hence change the frequency of the LA cycles within each quantal MMO rhythm without any change in the overall oscillation frequency of the 3-neuron population.
source: In contrast to changes in connection weights, a change in the excitability of the LE neuron alone could alter the V3-nullclines (for all input levels) and hence change the frequency of the LA cycles within each quantal MMO rhythm without any change in the overall oscillation frequency of the 3-neuron population (data not shown).
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis.

claim: An increase in the excitability of the HE neuron alone caused an increase of the SA burst frequency.
source: On the other hand, an increase in the excitability of the HE neuron alone caused an increase of the SA burst frequency.
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model analysis.

claim: IBIs were longer after LA bursts than after SA bursts in the MMOs observed in the large-scale model.
source: Another feature of the MMOs observed in our large-scale model is that IBIs were longer after LA bursts than after SA bursts.
evidence: This is a result from the large-scale model.

claim: Stronger excitation pushes a neuron's V-nullcline, including its right knee, to lower hNaP values and hence causes the active phase to end with more INaP inactivation.
source: Stronger excitation pushes a neuron's V-nullcline, including its right knee, to lower hNaP values and hence causes the active phase to end with more INaP inactivation (i.e., lower hNaP-coordinate).
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claim: A longer recovery period is needed before subsequent activation of the leading neuron when the active phase ends with more INaP inactivation.
source: Thus, a longer recovery period is needed before subsequent activation of the leading neuron.
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claim: On LA cycles, all neurons excite each other, which causes a maximal lowering of V-nullclines and subsequently yields the longest IBIs.
source: On LA cycles, all neurons excite each other, which causes a maximal lowering of V-nullclines and subsequently yields the longest IBIs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the reduced model analysis.

claim: Quiescence could be induced in the LE and ME neurons after decreasing all excitabilities by 8%.
source: Quiescence could be induced in the LE and ME neurons after decreasing all excitabilities by 8% (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A similar regime of only SA bursts could be produced by decreasing weights of neuronal interconnections.
source: A similar regime of only SA bursts could be produced by decreasing weights of neuronal interconnections (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a result from the reduced model shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The two key features formulated (reduction of spiking frequency within bursts with increasing burst frequency and dependence of after-burst recovery on burst amplitude) represent common properties of populations of intrinsically bursting neurons with distributed excitability that extend across many different bursting mechanisms.
source: Therefore the two key features formulated above, which are critical for generation of network-based MMOs, appear to represent common properties of populations of intrinsically bursting neurons with distributed excitability that extend across many different bursting mechanisms.
evidence: This is a generalization based on analysis of different bursting mechanisms.

claim: A progressive suppression of INaP in the pre-BötC in vitro by riluzole should cause a transitional MMO regime before abolishing rhythmicity completely.
source: We consider this result as a prediction for future experimental study, suggesting that a progressive suppression of INaP in the pre-BötC in vitro by its specific blocker, riluzole, should cause a transitional MMO regime before abolishing rhythmicity completely.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the computational model results.

claim: The effects of Cd2+ could either attenuate neuronal excitability or reduce excitatory synaptic interconnections within the pre-BötC.
source: We therefore suggest that the effects of Cd2+, a blocker of calcium currents, could either attenuate neuronal excitability or reduce excitatory synaptic interconnections within the pre-BötC, as seen in our simulations (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparison of model results with experimental observations.

claim: Neurons with low excitability, which generate low frequency bursting with high intra-burst spike frequency, recruit LA bursts by synchronizing the activity of many neurons in the network and therefore play a critical role in the generation of MMOs.
source: Our simulations and analysis suggest that neurons with low excitability, which generate low frequency bursting with high intra-burst spike frequency, recruit LA bursts by synchronizing the activity of many neurons in the network and therefore play a critical role in the generation of MMOs.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the computational modeling and analysis.

claim: Neurons with relatively high excitability (EL), and therefore with the high burst frequency (HE neurons), participated in some SA and all LA bursts.
source: Specifically, neurons with relatively high excitability (EL), and therefore with the high burst frequency (HE neurons), participated in some SA and all LA bursts
evidence: This is a result from the large-scale model analysis.

claim: Neurons with the lowest excitability and the lowest burst frequency (LE neurons) participated only in LA bursts.
source: whereas neurons with the lowest excitability and the lowest burst frequency (LE neurons) participated only in LA bursts.
evidence: This is a result from the large-scale model analysis.

claim: LE neurons had the highest spike frequency within the bursts and could provide the strongest excitatory synaptic inputs to other neurons, resulting in the network-wide synchronization underlying the generation of LA bursts.
source: Importantly, since LE neurons had the highest spike frequency (Figure 3B3) within the bursts, they could provide the strongest excitatory synaptic inputs to other neurons, resulting in the network-wide synchronization underlying the generation of LA bursts.
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the large-scale model analysis.

claim: A mechanism intrinsic to the LE neurons and connected with their slow recovery is critically involved in the generation of LA bursts, defining their IBIs and the output burst frequency.
source: This suggests that a mechanism intrinsic to the LE neurons and connected with their slow recovery is critically involved in the generation of LA bursts, defining their IBIs and the output burst frequency.
evidence: This is a key mechanistic conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: The strong mutual excitation that occurs during an LA burst is responsible for the pause in activity of the tonic spiking neurons after an LA burst in the large-scale model.
source: Interestingly, based on this analysis and previous work (Dunmyre and Rubin, 2010) we can infer that the strong mutual excitation, that occurs during an LA burst, is responsible for the pause in activity of the tonic spiking neurons after an LA burst in the large-scale model (Figure 3B2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the model analysis and prior work.

claim: Both the prolonged IBI and the pause in tonic spiking after LA bursts rely on the synaptic excitation from the full collection of neurons in the network.
source: Both the prolonged IBI and the pause in tonic spiking after LA bursts rely on the synaptic excitation from the full collection of neurons in the network
evidence: This is a mechanistic insight from the model analysis.

claim: The presence of prolonged IBI and pause in tonic spiking after LA bursts can be taken as evidence that the least excitable neurons in the network are not recipients of feed-forward inputs but rather participate in the recurrent network structure.
source: and thus their presence can be taken as evidence that the least excitable neurons in the network are not recipients of feed-forward inputs but rather participate in the recurrent network structure.
evidence: This is an inference about network structure based on model behavior.

claim: MMOs were artificially evoked at a moderate level of neuronal excitability produced by elevation of [K+]out to 5–6 mM in the study by Kam et al., 2013.
source: These MMOs were artificially evoked at a moderate level of neuronal excitability produced by elevation of [K+]out to 5–6 mM and were characterized by a series of SA bursts ('burstlets') alternating with single LA bursts that, in contrast to the burstlets, were able to trigger the rhythmic bursts in the hypoglossal motor output and hence defined the frequency of output oscillations.
evidence: This describes experimental conditions from a cited study.

claim: The study by Kam et al., 2013 established the quantal nature of MMOs emerging in the pre-BötC.
source: This study established the quantal nature of MMOs emerging in the pre-BötC in these conditions (e.g., Figure 2 of Kam et al., 2013).

claim: The computational study does not support the interpretation of MMOs in the pre-BötC as indicative of separate rhythm- and pattern-generating sub-networks.
source: Our computational study does not support the interpretation of MMOs in the pre-BötC as indicative of separate rhythm- (burstlets) and pattern- (bursts) generating sub-networks.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claim: A single, inseparable population of coupled excitatory neurons incorporating endogenous neuronal oscillators with distributed excitability can reproduce and is sufficient to explain the coexistence of burstlets and bursts in population rhythmic activity.
source: The results of our present modeling study instead suggest that a single, inseparable population of coupled excitatory neurons incorporating endogenous neuronal oscillators with distributed excitability can reproduce, and is sufficient to explain, the coexistence of burstlets and bursts in population rhythmic activity (i.e., the MMOs described in this work).
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claim: The activity of low-excitable neurons involved in generation of low frequency LA bursts synchronize the entire population activity, explicitly defining its output frequency.
source: In contrast, in the interconnected single network considered here, the activity of low-excitable neurons involved in generation of low frequency LA bursts (attributed by Kam et al. to the 'pattern generating circuits') synchronize the entire population activity, explicitly defining its output frequency ('rhythm').
evidence: This is a key mechanistic conclusion from the model.

claim: The intrinsic properties of low-excitable neurons, specifically the temporal characteristics of their recovery, define the output frequency of a rhythm generator.
source: Therefore, the intrinsic properties of these low-excitable neurons, specifically the temporal characteristics of their recovery (see Figures 5D1,D2 and 6B), but not deletions of unknown origin, define the output frequency of a rhythm generator that interacts with other circuits to shape the CPG activity pattern.
evidence: This is a key mechanistic conclusion from the model analysis.

source: INaP has been found in pre-BötC neurons and the rhythmic bursting activity in the pre-BötC could be abolished by pharmacological blockade of this current (Del Negro et al., 2002a; Rybak et al., 2003a; Rybak et al., 2003b; Hayes et al., 2008)

claim: Del Negro et al., 2005 suggested that INaP may be the primary rhythm-generating current up to postnatal day 4 or 5 (P4 or P5), after which ICAN is also expressed and strongly contributes to rhythm generation.
source: Del Negro et al., 2005 suggested that INaP may be the primary rhythm-generating current up to postnatal day 4 or 5 (P4 or P5), after which ICAN is also expressed and strongly contributes to rhythm generation.

claim: All currently available data on MMOs were obtained in slices from neonatal animals within the developmental range in which INaP is considered to be the primary rhythm-generating current.
source: However, all currently available data on MMOs, including the early data (Koshiya and Smith, 1999; Johnson et al., 2001) illustrated here (see Figure 1) and the recent data presented by Kam and Feldman (Kam et al., 2013; Feldman and Kam, 2015), were obtained, respectively, in slices from the neonatal animals of P0-P2, P0-P3, and P0-P5, i.e. within the developmental range in which INaP is considered to be the primary rhythm-generating current, supporting the inclusion of INaP in our models.
evidence: This is an argument supporting the modeling approach based on cited experimental data.

claim: The two key features (reduction of spiking frequency within bursts with increasing burst frequency and voltage-dependent slow recovery) result directly from INaP kinetics in the models.
source: However, although these key features in both of our models result directly from INaP kinetics, they actually are not specific to the INaP-dependent bursting mechanism analyzed herein.
evidence: This is an observation about the model properties.

claim: The two key features represent a common feature of most known cellular bursting mechanisms, in which the post-burst recovery time depends on the neuronal activity within the bursts and vice versa.
source: Instead, they represent a common feature of most known cellular bursting mechanisms, in which the post-burst recovery time depends on the neuronal activity within the bursts and vice versa.
evidence: This is a generalization based on knowledge of bursting mechanisms.

claim: In bursting mechanisms based on Ca2+-dependent potassium, Ca2+-activated nonspecific, or Na+-dependent potassium currents, a functionally similar slow recovery is usually connected with operation of either the Ca2+ or Na+/K+ pumps.
source: For example, in the case of intrinsic bursting mechanisms based on Ca2+-dependent potassium (IK(Ca2+)), Ca2+-activated nonspecific (ICAN), or Na+-dependent potassium (IK(Na+)) currents, involving intracellular accumulation of Ca2+ or Na+ ions, a functionally similar slow recovery is usually connected with operation of either the Ca2+ or Na+/K+ pumps (Ekeberg et al., 1991; el Manira et al., 1994; Wallén et al., 2007; Rubin et al., 2009a; Ryczko et al., 2010; Dunmyre and Rubin, 2010; Jasinski et al., 2013; Rybak et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work on bursting mechanisms.

claim: The conclusion that the two key features are common properties of populations of intrinsically bursting neurons contradicts the opinion published by Feldman and Kam, 2015 that previous computational models reproducing MMOs are not valid because neuronal bursting is critically dependent on slow deactivation kinetics of INaP.
source: This conclusion clearly contradicts a recently published opinion (Feldman and Kam, 2015) that previous computational models reproducing the MMOs observed in the pre-BötC (e.g., Butera et al., 1999b; Rybak et al., 2004) are not valid because the neuronal bursting in these models is critically dependent on slow deactivation kinetics of INaP.
evidence: This is a statement of disagreement with a published opinion, supported by the modeling results.
